sar.narrative: This Suspicious Activity Report details a series of unauthorized online card-not-present transactions involving customer C01104 and primary card C01104-K2. Between 04:00:52 and 04:18:01 UTC on November 15, 2016, four online purchases for product H totaling $600.10 were executed in rapid succession across an 18-minute window. The transactions consisted of four authorizations in nearly identical amounts: transaction 3459139 ($150.08), transaction 3459152 ($150.07), transaction 3459154 ($150.03), and transaction 3459158 ($149.92). Each transaction was submitted from the online channel using a different billing region (regions 184, 441, 299, and 494), demonstrating systematic manipulation or spoofing of billing address data. The authorizations were conducted using device D007387, identified as an iOS Device running iOS 11.3.0 with mobile safari generic at 1334x750 resolution. Device D007387 was flagged as new to card C01104-K2 during transaction 3459154 and possesses a high fraud lift of 6.92 in the seven-day observation window. Cross-entity graph analysis revealed that device D007387 directly connects card C01104-K2 to card C02354-K2, which utilized the same device behind a transparent proxy (transaction 3441751) amid concurrent confirmed fraud. Card C01104-K2 also has six prior confirmed fraud cases, including case CC-5037 involving an identical $149.91 purchase on a mobile Safari device, and is associated with suspicious device ring 40894916. The combination of rapid velocity, rotating billing regions, cross-card links to proxy activity, and historical compromise patterns indicates coordinated card-not-present fraud from an unauthorized device. In response, the bank blocked card C01104-K2 to mitigate exposure and placed connected card C02354-K2 under automated monitoring.

answer.stop_reason: Under policy section 6, the investigation was concluded because the fraud probability reached 0.97, decisively exceeding the 0.85 threshold based on more than two independent incriminating signals (calibrated model score, rapid burst timing, rotating billing regions, device cross-card links, and prior fraud history), meaning further steps would not alter the outcome.

passages.section: Section 3a. A case is not a report
passages.text: Section 3a. A case is not a report. Two different things, and the agent produces both. **A case** (`CREATE_CASE`) is the bank's internal record of an investigation. Open one whenever fraud probability reaches 0.30, whenever you request evidence, or whenever a customer disputes a charge. A case can be closed as fraud or as legitimate. It can be updated when new evidence arrives. It should be written into the graph so later investigations can find it: a case that names a merchant or a device becomes evidence for the next analyst. **A suspicious activity report** (`FILE_REPORT`) is a regulatory filing sent outside the bank. File one when fraud is confirmed or strongly suspected **and** at least one of these holds: exposure exceeds $1,000; the activity connects to a shared device profile, a shared region cluster, or another customer's fraud; the pattern is coordinated or undocumented (rule R9). A report always has a case behind it. Most cases never need a report. The report narrative must stand on its own: who, what, when, where, how, and why it is suspicious. Deciding correctly between ""case only"" and ""case plus report"" is part of the next-best-action score.

Rule R6: Shared origin. When several cards show fraud from the same device profile, the same billing region, or the same recipient email in one window, name the shared element, recommend `CREATE_CASE` and `FILE_REPORT`, and `MONITOR_CONNECTED_CARDS` for every card that shares it.

assessment.reasoning: Investigation of transaction 3459158 ($149.92 on card C01104-K2) reveals a textbook card-not-present fraud episode originating from a new device. Although the legacy risk score was low at 0.19, the second-generation model scored this authorization at 0.998, which is historically associated with a 92.1% fraud rate. Examination of the card activity shows that the flagged transaction is the final authorization in a rapid burst of 4 online purchases occurring within an 18-minute window on the morning of 2016-11-15 (between 04:00:52 and 04:18:01), all for product H and almost identical amounts (~$150.00 each: $150.08, $150.07, $150.03, $149.92), totaling $600.10. Each authorization in this burst specified a different billing region (184, 441, 299, 494), indicating spoofed or manipulated address details. The burst utilized device D007387, which was marked New for this account. In the 7-day window, device D007387 exhibits a hot fraud share of 0.1429 (lift of 6.92 vs baseline) and connects card C01104-K2 to card C02354-K2, which used the same device behind a transparent proxy (tx 3441751) amid extensive fraud. Card C01104-K2 also has 6 prior confirmed fraud cases, including CC-5037 ($149.91 on an iOS generic device under card_not_present_new_device) and belongs to suspicious device ring 40894916 alongside serial fraud card C03278-K2. Although device D007387 has a generic profile with no historical closed cases, and card C01104-K2 has one cleared travel case (CC-0862), the combination of calibrated model score, rapid burst sequence, rotating billing regions, cross-card proxy link, and identical historical fraud pattern decisively establishes fraud.
